notes:
These notes cover most of Proverbs 12, verse by verse. I ran out of research steps before reaching some sources, so a few areas are thin. I didn't get to any Catholic or Orthodox sites (newadvent, catholic.com, oca.org), bibleodyssey.org, or the denominational sites in your list (ligonier, desiringgod, seedbed, lcms and so on). I also found no page describing a prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace reading of any verse, so those are left out. The "Catholic/older readings" points below come only from the Latin Vulgate and Greek Septuagint renderings that the older commentaries report, plus Douay-Rheims wording shown on Bible Hub. The tradition labels I give the older writers (Gill Baptist, Clarke Methodist, Henry Presbyterian, Keil–Delitzsch Lutheran) are my own; the pages don't state them.

**v. 1**
- Guzik: being willing to be taught shows a real love of knowledge. Rejecting correction shows pride. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-12/
- MacLaren: hating reproof is "brutish" quite literally. Animals don't understand the purpose of pain, so they never improve. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/12-1.htm
- Clarke: the Hebrew word means such a man is like a bear. He gets no more from correction than an ox does from the goad. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-12.html
- Pulpit: quotes Augustine (*On Rebuke and Grace*): the person who refuses correction needs correcting for that very refusal. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/12.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik: God sees wicked intentions even if they never become actions. He adds that blessing for obedience applied especially under the old covenant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-12/
- Tradition note, Clarke (Methodist): he puts grace first. God makes a man good, since everyone is bad until grace changes the heart. Then, as he obeys, he grows in goodness and in God's favour. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-12.html
- Pulpit: "good" here means pure, a heart free of evil schemes. The Septuagint says the sinner will be "passed over in silence." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/12.htm

**v. 3**
- Clarke: the righteous have their root in God, which is why they cannot be moved. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-12.html
- Pulpit: the image is a tree, especially an olive. It links this to being "rooted and grounded in love" (Eph 3:17). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/12.htm

**v. 4**
- Guzik, citing Kidner: the Hebrew word means strength and worth, not just "virtuous." Waltke: the shameful wife weakens her husband from within. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-12/
- Bible Hub study notes: the same Hebrew phrase, *'eshet chayil*, describes the Proverbs 31 woman. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/proverbs/12.htm
- Clarke: he takes "strong woman" partly literally, as physical strength. He links "rottenness in his bones" to an unfaithful wife. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-12.html

**v. 5**
- Matthew Henry: thoughts are not "free"; God judges them. A good man may have bad suggestions come to mind, but he doesn't nurse them into plans. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_012.cfm
- Pulpit: Gregory the Great read "judgments" as conscience. The righteous judge their own sins inwardly ahead of the Day of Judgment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/12.htm

**v. 6**
- Pulpit: the wicked endanger lives by false witness, as Jezebel did to Naboth. The upright rescue the innocent by speaking up for them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/12.htm
- Bridgeway: the righteous have the courage to speak up at risk to themselves in order to save others. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/proverbs-12.html

**v. 7**
- Pulpit: the verb could mean "turn the wicked," so the slightest blow overthrows them. It compares the house that stands to the wise builder in Matthew 7:24. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/12.htm
- Clarke: God blesses the families of the righteous, while wicked family lines tend to be cut off. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-12.html

**v. 8**
- Guzik: this is often true now and always true in the age to come. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-12/
- MacLaren: hypocrites exist only because people secretly rank wisdom highest, and that proves the proverb. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/12-1.htm

**v. 9**
- Pulpit: the Hebrew literally says "a servant to himself," meaning someone who supplies his own needs. The Vulgate and Septuagint agree. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/12.htm
- Clarke follows the Vulgate: better a poor man who provides for himself than a proud man without bread. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-12.html
- Guzik notes Kidner's alternative ("works for himself"), which the RSV takes from the Septuagint. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-12/

**v. 10**
- Pulpit: "regards" literally means "knows," so he understands what his animals need. It lists the Mosaic laws protecting animals, such as Sabbath rest and not muzzling the ox. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/12.htm
- Clarke: one principal characteristic of a holy man is mercy. Even the "mercies" of the wicked are a cover for cruelty. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-12.html

**v. 11**
- Pulpit: the second half is about "vain things," useless pursuits. The Vulgate's "he who studies ease" doesn't fit the Hebrew. The Septuagint and Vulgate also add a line about drinking that isn't in the Hebrew. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/12.htm

**v. 12** (the Hebrew is hard here)
- Pulpit: scholars have tried to correct the text, but the Hebrew as it stands makes sense. The key word could mean the "net," the "prey," or a "fortress." Pulpit prefers "prey": the wicked want the loot that other sinners take. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/12.htm
- Guzik: the righteous don't need to covet, because fruit comes from their own root. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-12/

**v. 13**
- Clarke: liars are eventually caught; "a liar had need of a good memory." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-12.html
- Guzik: the righteous will have trouble but come through it (John 16:33). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-12/

**v. 14**
- Keil–Delitzsch (via Bible Hub): the proverb finds its final verification in the last judgment (cf. Matthew 12:37), but it is also illustrated in the present life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/12-14.htm
- Tradition note, Gill (Baptist): God's repayment for works serves not to establish the doctrine of merit, but to show the goodness and grace of God in accepting imperfect works for Christ's sake. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/12-14.htm
- NET note: "lips" stands for speech; proper speech will result in good things. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=pro&chapter=12&verse=14
- Bible Hub's own study note: it calls this not mere positivity. It is a principle God built in: speak what is right and he supplies good. This was the nearest thing I found to the "power of words" theme; I found no source describing a word-of-faith reading. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/12-14.htm

**v. 15**
- Guzik: fools almost always think they're on the right path. The wise get another set of "eyes" on their life. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-12/

**v. 16**
- Henry: a wise man may be angry for good reason, but he rules his anger; a fool's anger rules him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_012.cfm
- Clarke: "A fool's bolt is soon shot." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-12.html
- Guzik, quoting Ross: the wise man handles anger shrewdly rather than simply bottling it up. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-12/

**v. 17**
- Pett: the true witness upholds what is right, and so supports justice. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/proverbs-12.html

**v. 18**
- Henry: insults, slander and whispering wound like a sword, sometimes beyond repair, and they cut apart friendships. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_012.cfm
- Bible Hub study notes: the Hebrew word for "healing" (*marpe*) suggests restoration. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/proverbs/12.htm
- Pulpit: the Vulgate narrows this to someone who makes rash promises and is then stung by conscience. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/12.htm

**v. 19**
- Clarke: truth stands because its foundation can't be destroyed. A lie gets credit only while people think it's true. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-12.html
- Guzik: measured against eternity, lies last only a moment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-12/

**v. 20**
- Henry: those who plot harm to deceive others end up deceiving themselves. Deceivers will be deceived. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_012.cfm

**v. 21** (commentators qualify "no harm")
- Pulpit: the "harm" meant is not misfortune in general but the evil consequences that follow on ill-doing. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/12-21.htm
- Clarke and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown read it through Romans 8:28: God turns everything to the good of the righteous. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/12-21.html
- Tradition note, Gill (Baptist): no punishment for sin will fall on the righteous, because it was laid on Christ their surety. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/12-21.htm
- Older/Catholic reading: the Vulgate (Douay-Rheims) says nothing that happens will make the just man sad. The Septuagint says no injustice will please the just man. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/12-21.htm

**v. 22**
- Pett: lies go against the very fabric of creation, while those who deal truly are God's delight. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/proverbs-12.html

**v. 23**
- Henry: the wise man shares knowledge when it helps others, but holds it back when showing it would only promote himself. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_012.cfm
- Pett: he doesn't hide knowledge from sincere seekers, only from those who would mock or misuse it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/proverbs-12.html

**v. 24**
- Clarke: the diligent rule because their work makes them independent. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-12.html
- Pett: Solomon treats the diligent as the righteous and wise, and the lazy as the unrighteous fool. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/proverbs-12.html

**v. 25**
- Clarke: one kind word can lift despondency. The word "Son, be of good cheer, thy sins are forgiven" can lift even despair. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-12.html
- Pulpit: Christians are told to beware of too much anxiety. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/12.htm

**v. 26** (the meaning of the first line is disputed)
- NET: "cautious in his friendship." It notes another option, "the righteous guides his friend aright" (cf. NRSV, NLT). https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Pro&chapter=12&verse=26
- Pulpit prefers "a guide to his neighbour." Keil–Delitzsch read "looks after his pasture." Luther translated "better than his neighbour." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/12-26.htm
- Tradition note, Gill (Baptist): the righteous man excels because Christ's imputed righteousness is far better than his neighbour's own. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/12-26.html
- Clarke: the poor righteous man is better than his rich, sinful neighbour. He notes the Vulgate (Catholic) reading: a man who takes a loss for a friend's sake is just. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-12.html

**v. 27**
- Clarke: the key word properly means "fraudulent," so God snatches away what was gained dishonestly. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-12.html
- Pett: the diligent enjoy roasted game while the lazy waste theirs. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/proverbs-12.html

**v. 28** (does it teach immortality?)
- Keil–Delitzsch (Lutheran), siding with Luther and the older interpreters, read "the way of its path is immortality." They see Proverbs beginning to announce a life beyond the reach of death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/12-28.htm
- Pulpit is more cautious: the writer probably believed it, but this verse alone can't prove it. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/12-28.htm
- Tradition note, Gill (Baptist): "no death" means no condemnation to them that are in Christ. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/amp/proverbs/12-28.html
- Tradition note, Clarke (Methodist): every duty and act of faith "leads to life"; "the path of duty is the way of safety." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-12.html
- Older/Catholic reading: the Septuagint, Vulgate and some Hebrew copies read "leads to death," which is the BSB/NET wording. Douay-Rheims has "the by-way leadeth to death." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/12-28.htm
